title: Teaching a junior doctor a clinical skill: interrupted suturing

guidelineVersions: UK Foundation Programme Curriculum 2021: supervised learning events
Giacomino et al., PeerJ 2020 (Peyton's four-step approach)
Health and Safety (Sharp Instruments in Healthcare) Regulations 2013

related.id: MB-180 Interrupted suturing and wound closure on a skin pad
related.why: The suturing technique itself, taught here
The instrument tie used in the demonstration

brief.scenario: Dr Lucy Fairweather is a foundation year 1 doctor on your surgical firm. She has watched suturing but never done it herself, and has asked you to teach her. A skin pad with an incision, a suture pack, a needle holder, toothed forceps, scissors, 3-0 nylon and a sharps bin are provided.
brief.task: Teach Dr Fairweather to place and tie a simple interrupted suture on the skin pad. The examiner may ask you questions at the end.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Teach, don't just demonstrate: find her starting point, use a structured method, watch her do it, and give specific feedback.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Doing a running commentary while suturing, then saying "your turn".
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "What have you seen or done so far, and what would you like to get out of this?"

grid.label: Learner's needs and objective
grid.fail: Starts demonstrating without asking what she knows.
grid.pass: Asks what she has seen or done, and agrees what she'll be able to do by the end.
grid.high: Sets a specific, achievable objective and asks how she's feeling about it; picks up her anxiety.

grid.label: Demonstration (step 1)
grid.fail: No demonstration, or a rushed one with no explanation of structure.
grid.pass: Explains the plan, then demonstrates one full suture at normal speed without commentary.
grid.high: Explains why: she first sees what the whole skill looks like done well.

grid.label: Deconstruction (step 2)
grid.fail: Skips the breakdown, or gives it in jargon.
grid.pass: Repeats slowly, naming each step: grip, perpendicular entry, following the needle's curve, even bites, instrument tie.
grid.high: Flags the safety-critical steps: needle handled only with instruments, never recapped, into the sharps bin at the point of use.

grid.label: Comprehension (step 3)
grid.fail: Moves straight to her attempt without checking understanding.
grid.pass: Performs a third suture while she talks the candidate through each step, correcting any gaps.
grid.high: Asks "why" at key steps (why evert? why hold the needle there?) to check understanding, not memory.

grid.label: Supervised performance and safety (step 4)
grid.fail: Lets her handle the needle with her fingers, or takes over without explanation.
grid.pass: Watches her suture; stops her at once, calmly, when she reaches for the needle with her fingers, then lets her continue.
grid.high: Separates immediate safety correction from developmental points, which wait for the feedback.

grid.label: Feedback
grid.pass: Asks her self-assessment first; specific, behaviour-based points on what went well and one or two to improve.
grid.high: Agrees an action plan: more practice on the pad, then supervised suturing on a patient.

grid.label: Competence and supervision
grid.fail: Agrees she can suture alone in ED tonight, or signs off what the candidate hasn't seen.
grid.pass: Not yet independent: supervised practice on patients first; records only what the candidate directly observed.
grid.high: Knows a DOPS is a supervised learning event, not a pass or licence; supervision is graded to competence.

grid.label: Teaching principles and evidence
grid.fail: Cannot name a structured method, or says "see one, do one, teach one" is enough.
grid.pass: Names Peyton's four steps: demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension, performance.
grid.high: Cites 2020 meta-analysis of RCTs: effective for procedural skills, especially small groups with faculty teachers; not a fixed rule.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Right, watch me. You grab the needle, go in here, out there, then tie it like this. Got it? Your turn.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Dr Fairweather picks the needle up with her fingers to straighten it.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Careful. Actually, let me just do it, it's quicker.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Dr Fairweather: "Can you sign a DOPS so I can do them on nights?"

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Sure, you've got the idea now.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What teaching method did you use?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: See one, do one, teach one. That's how I learned.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hi Lucy. What have you seen or done before? By the end, I'd like you to place and tie an interrupted suture yourself. I'll show you first, then break it down, then you'll talk me through it, then you'll do it.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Candidate demonstrates one suture at normal speed, in silence.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Now slowly. Hold the needle two-thirds back from the tip. Enter at ninety degrees, follow the curve, equal bites each side. Then an instrument tie.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: This time you tell me each step while I do it.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Dr Fairweather talks the candidate through; the candidate corrects her on bite depth.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: She starts her own suture and reaches for the needle with her fingers.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Stop there, please. Use the forceps for the needle, never fingers. That's it, carry on.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: How do you think that went? Your entry angle was spot on. Next time, take slightly bigger bites so the edges evert.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Dr Fairweather: "Can you sign me off so I can suture on nights?"

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not yet. I can record what I watched today, but you need supervised practice on patients before suturing alone.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Peyton's four steps: demonstration, deconstruction, comprehension and performance.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hi Lucy. What have you seen or done so far, and how are you feeling about it?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Dr Fairweather: "Nervous. I'm not very good with my hands."

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's normal; this is exactly how everyone starts. Our goal: by the end, you'll place and tie one interrupted suture on your own, safely. First I'll do one at normal speed without talking, so you see what the whole thing looks like.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Now step by step. The needle is only ever touched with instruments. It goes in perpendicular, and I rotate my wrist to follow its curve. When I'm done it goes straight into this sharps bin, never recapped.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Now you talk me through it. Why do you think we evert the edges?

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: She starts her own suture and reaches for the needle with her fingers.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Pause. Forceps, not fingers, for the needle. Good, carry on. I'll save my other points for afterwards.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: What went well, and what would you change? I agree, your entry angle was good. Two things: bigger bites so the edges evert, and a flat square first throw. Plan: ten more on the pad, then I'll supervise you on a patient this week.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Dr Fairweather: "Can you sign a DOPS so I can do them on nights?"

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'll record a DOPS for what I saw today, but it's a learning event, not a pass. Suturing without supervision comes once you've done several well with me watching.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Is there evidence for this method?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: A 2020 meta-analysis of randomised trials found Peyton's approach effective for procedural skills, particularly in small groups taught by faculty. It isn't the only valid method; see one, do one isn't enough.

failures.move: Ignoring her handling the needle with her fingers.
failures.consequence: A needlestick risk now, and a habit that carries into practice on patients.

failures.move: Signing her off to suture alone after one attempt on a pad.
failures.consequence: Supervision must match demonstrated competence; a single observed attempt doesn't show that.
She learns nothing specific and repeats her errors.

failures.move: Starting to demonstrate without asking what she knows.
failures.consequence: The teaching may be pitched wrongly, and her anxiety goes unaddressed.

recovery.when: You've started demonstrating without setting up
recovery.line: Let me pause: what have you done before, and what would you like to get from this?
Stop there for a second. Let's fix that before you carry on.

knowledge.fact: Peyton's four steps: demonstration in real time; deconstruction with explanation; comprehension (learner talks teacher through); performance by the learner.
Supervisors determine the learner's competence and grade supervision to it (R1.9); learners get regular, constructive feedback (R3.13).
DOPS is a foundation supervised learning event: formative, cannot be passed or failed.
Be accurate, fair and objective when assessing colleagues (para 62).
Needles are not recapped after use; sharps containers sit close to where sharps are used (reg 5).

recall.think: A needlestick now, or an unsafe doctor on nights later.
recall.say: "What have you done before, and what do you want from this?"
do: Stop unsafe moves; feedback and plan
recall.trap: One good attempt on a pad isn't competence.
recall.finish: Action plan: pad practice, then supervised suturing on patients.

sources.name: Giacomino K, Caliesch R, Sattelmayer KM. The effectiveness of the Peyton's 4-step teaching approach on skill acquisition of procedures in health professions education: a systematic review and meta-analysis with integrated meta-regression. PeerJ 2020;8:e10129 (PMID 33083149)

sources.name: GMC: Promoting excellence: standards for medical education and training
sources.supports: Appropriate clinical supervision at all times (R1.8); supervision graded to the learner's competence, confidence and experience (R1.9); regular, constructive and meaningful feedback (R3.13); educators trained and supported (R4.1)

sources.name: GMC: Good medical practice 2024 (Domain 3: Colleagues, culture and safety)
sources.supports: Appropriate supervision of colleagues whose work you oversee (para 61); accurate, fair and objective assessment (para 62); willingness to support colleagues through teaching and training

sources.name: UK Foundation Programme: Curriculum 2021, Supervised learning events (introduction)
sources.supports: SLEs (including DOPS) are interactions leading to immediate feedback and reflection; they are not assessments and cannot be passed or failed

sources.supports: Needles not recapped after use (reg 5(1)(c)); secure sharps containers located close to where sharps are used (reg 5(1)(d))

partner.opening: Dr Fairweather is at the skin pad with the suture pack open. Please begin.
partner.actorBrief: You are Dr Lucy Fairweather, a foundation year 1 doctor, four months into your surgical job. You have watched suturing a few times but never done it. You are keen but anxious: last week a registrar laughed at your knot tying in theatre. Opening line: "Thanks for doing this. I'm on ED nights next month and I'd love to be able to suture." Reveal your nerves only if asked how you feel: "Nervous. I'm not very good with my hands." During step 3, forget to mention bite depth unless prompted. During your own attempt, reach for the needle with your fingers to straighten it; if stopped kindly, correct it and carry on. Take slightly shallow bites. If asked to assess yourself, say: "The knot felt OK but the edges look a bit flat." Near the end ask: "Can you sign a DOPS so I can do them on nights?" If the candidate is patient and specific, you become more confident.

reveals.finding: "Nervous. A registrar laughed at my knots last week."

reveals.trigger: Asks her to talk through the steps
reveals.finding: She describes the grip and entry well but leaves out bite depth.
"The knot felt OK but the edges look a bit flat."

push.question: What teaching method did you use, and is there evidence for it?
push.expect: Peyton's four steps; a 2020 meta-analysis of RCTs found it effective for procedural skills, especially small groups.

push.question: How would you decide she can suture unsupervised?
push.expect: Several directly observed procedures on patients done safely; DOPS as learning events with feedback; supervision graded to competence.

curveballs.prompt: "Could you just do all the steps quickly? I learn best by watching."
curveballs.safeAnswer: Acknowledges her preference but explains she needs to talk it through and perform it herself to learn it safely.

curveballs.prompt: She becomes tearful after the correction.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Pauses, acknowledges it, normalises the mistake, and asks whether she wants to carry on; keeps feedback private and kind.

curveballs.prompt: "There are three of us who want to learn. Can you teach us all at once?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes, in a small group, with each doing supervised practice; the four-step approach can be adapted for small groups.
